name: Policy Framing for Resilience
consequences: Reframing digital identity dependencies as a resilience risk rather than a privacy issue could shift institutional priorities toward contingency planning. However, this approach risks diluting the sovereignty argument if resilience metrics are not explicitly tied to supplier concentration and geopolitical exposure.
options: Anchor policy proposals in national security frameworks by linking platform dependencies to critical infrastructure resilience requirements
Develop a standardized risk-assessment matrix for public-sector digital services that explicitly quantifies supplier concentration exposure
Leverage recent EU Digital Identity Wallet guidelines to reframe Danish procurement requirements as a compliance imperative
review: Prioritizing resilience metrics risks overshadowing sovereignty concerns; the three options fail to address how to counter convenience-driven arguments from incumbent providers.

name: Technical Demonstrators as Standards Advocacy
consequences: Creating non-production demonstrators proves technical feasibility of platform-neutral solutions but may be dismissed as academic exercises without institutional buy-in. This risks reinforcing the perception that alternatives lack operational credibility.
options: Build a FIDO2/WebAuthn demonstrator using GrapheneOS that mimics MitID workflows while highlighting platform independence
Develop a browser-based authentication prototype requiring no OS-level trust signals to challenge existing integrity assumptions
Create a hardware-token workflow that bypasses mobile OS ecosystems entirely for high-assurance transactions
review: Demonstrators may lack operational credibility; the options leave unaddressed how to transition from proof-of-concept to institutional adoption.

name: Stakeholder Coalition Expansion
consequences: Broadening the coalition beyond privacy advocates to include business interests and technical experts could increase influence but risks diluting the core sovereignty message through conflicting priorities.
options: Form an industry-academia partnership with Danish fintech firms to co-develop platform-neutral authentication use cases
Engage cybersecurity researchers in threat-modeling exercises that expose vulnerabilities in current platform-dependent architectures
Create a cross-sector working group with public-sector IT managers to identify pain points in current identity infrastructure
review: Coalition expansion risks mission drift; the options fail to address how to maintain focus on supplier concentration amid diverse stakeholder interests.

name: Regulatory Pressure through EU Channels
consequences: Aligning with EU digital identity initiatives could amplify influence but may require compromising on national sovereignty priorities to meet broader European standards.
options: Influence European Digital Identity Wallet specifications to include mandatory fallback authentication requirements
Leverage EU procurement directives to challenge platform-specific identity requirements in member states
Collaborate with Nordic regulatory bodies to create a regional framework for platform-neutral identity solutions
review: EU alignment risks diluting national priorities; the options leave unaddressed how to maintain distinct Danish sovereignty goals within broader European frameworks.

name: Procurement Language Influence
consequences: Shaping procurement requirements to mandate platform neutrality could create lasting change but may face resistance from vendors and public-sector buyers accustomed to existing ecosystems.
options: Draft procurement clauses requiring identity solutions to demonstrate compliance with open-standard authentication protocols
Push for mandatory third-party audit requirements that evaluate supplier concentration risks in identity infrastructure
Develop a certification framework for platform-neutral identity solutions that could be adopted by public-sector buyers
review: Procurement changes face implementation delays; the options leave unaddressed how to overcome existing vendor lock-in and institutional preferences.

name: Alternative Authentication Ecosystem Development
consequences: Building non-platform authentication methods creates viable alternatives but risks fragmentation if standards lack interoperability. Direct adoption depends on convincing public-sector stakeholders to prioritize resilience over convenience, with downstream implications for vendor lock-in dynamics.
options: Develop open-source hardware tokens for secure authentication
Partner with Danish banks to implement SMS-based fallback mechanisms
Integrate with IoT devices for multi-factor authentication
review: Prioritizing hardware tokens risks scalability due to hardware costs, while SMS fallback may lack security, leaving a gap in robust authentication for critical services.

name: Public-Private Partnership Agreements
consequences: Forming alliances with private entities accelerates resource sharing but may dilute focus on independent resilience. Success hinges on aligning commercial incentives with public-sector continuity goals, though conflicting priorities could stall progress.
options: Create joint R&D funds to support Danish startups in identity solutions
Establish co-branded identity platforms with local financial institutions
Develop shared infrastructure for authentication services
review: Public-private partnerships may prioritize commercial interests over public resilience, leaving gaps in oversight for non-commercial use cases.

name: Regulatory Compliance Mapping
consequences: Identifying regulatory loopholes enables targeted advocacy but requires navigating complex bureaucratic processes. Immediate gains depend on translating findings into enforceable policy, with risks of delayed implementation if stakeholders resist change.
options: Audit existing regulations for clauses that support platform-neutral solutions
Lobby for mandatory fallback authentication in public-sector contracts
Develop compliance checklists for developers to ensure adherence
review: Focusing on regulatory audits may delay implementation, while lobbying efforts risk being sidelined by more powerful stakeholders, leaving gaps in actionable policy changes.

name: Academic Collaboration Networks
consequences: Engaging universities drives innovation but may prioritize theoretical frameworks over practical deployment. Sustaining momentum requires bridging research gaps with real-world constraints, which could slow tangible outcomes.
options: Launch research initiatives on open standards for digital identity
Develop specialized curricula for digital identity security
Host workshops to connect industry experts with researchers
review: Academic focus may prioritize theoretical solutions over practical deployment, leaving gaps in real-world implementation strategies.

name: EU Funding Leverage
consequences: Securing EU grants provides resources but may divert focus toward compliance over innovation. Alignment with broader agendas could dilute localized resilience goals, though it offers credibility for policy advocacy.
options: Apply for Horizon Europe grants to support platform-neutral solutions
Partner with EU consortia to co-develop standards
Align project proposals with the European Digital Identity Framework
review: EU funding dependencies may shift priorities toward compliance over innovation, leaving gaps in localized resilience strategies.

name: Decentralized Identity Protocols
consequences: Adopting decentralized identity protocols reduces reliance on centralized platform trust models but introduces complexity in user onboarding and system interoperability. This shift risks fragmenting existing digital service ecosystems unless accompanied by mandatory integration mandates.
options: Implement FIDO2-based decentralized authentication frameworks across public-sector pilot services
Develop open-source identity verification modules compatible with non-proprietary OS distributions
Collaborate with Nordic blockchain initiatives to create a trust-layer interoperability standard
review: Decentralized protocols increase technical complexity and require stakeholder retraining, but leave gaps in interoperability with existing legacy systems.

name: Alternative Ecosystem Partnerships
consequences: Forming partnerships with non-traditional tech providers diversifies authentication channels but creates dependency on unproven alternatives that may lack enterprise-grade security certifications.
options: Establish collaboration with open-source mobile OS developers to create platform-neutral authentication middleware
Partner with regional telecom providers to develop SIM-based authentication fallback mechanisms
Engage with European open-source foundations to co-design identity verification standards
review: Ecosystem partnerships introduce untested alternatives that may lack enterprise security certifications, leaving gaps in regulatory compliance and service continuity.

name: Infrastructure Resilience Collaboration
consequences: Creating shared resilience frameworks among public-sector agencies strengthens collective preparedness but requires compromising on proprietary system requirements that favor incumbent platforms.
options: Co-develop cross-agency contingency authentication protocols with fallback to hardware tokens
Establish a centralized identity verification sandbox for testing platform-neutral solutions
Create joint procurement guidelines requiring multi-path authentication architecture
review: Resilience collaboration demands system architecture compromises that may delay immediate implementation, leaving gaps in urgent service continuity needs.

name: Open-Source Identity Frameworks
consequences: Building open-source identity solutions fosters transparency and customization but requires sustained community investment that may not align with institutional procurement timelines.
options: Launch a public repository for platform-neutral authentication reference implementations
Fund academic research on open-standard identity verification algorithms
Create a developer ecosystem for third-party authentication plugin integrations
review: Open-source development requires long-term commitment that may not match institutional procurement cycles, leaving gaps in immediate deployment capabilities.

name: Nordic Interoperability Consortium
consequences: Forming a Nordic consortium for identity standards harmonization strengthens regional influence but risks diluting technical requirements through consensus-driven compromises.
options: Establish a cross-border identity verification testing framework for Nordic public services
Coordinate joint procurement language to mandate multi-platform authentication support
Create shared technical review panels for identity system certifications
review: Consortium efforts may lead to watered-down standards that fail to challenge dominant platform requirements, leaving gaps in true technical independence.

name: Cross-Border Standards Advocacy
consequences: Promoting European-wide identity standards increases regulatory influence but requires navigating conflicting national interests that may slow implementation.
options: Lobby EU technical committees for mandatory fallback authentication requirements in digital identity frameworks
Align Danish demonstrator architectures with upcoming eIDAS3 interoperability mandates
Create joint technical working groups with Baltic and Nordic states for identity resilience planning
review: Cross-border advocacy risks dilution through national interest negotiations, leaving gaps in enforceable technical requirements for platform neutrality.

name: Public Infrastructure Resilience
consequences: Upgrading public infrastructure to support alternative authentication methods enhances service continuity but requires significant upfront investment in legacy system modifications.
options: Install hardware token verification endpoints in public service centers and municipal offices
Develop cloud-based identity verification systems with multi-path authentication support
Create regional backup authentication hubs for critical public services
review: Infrastructure upgrades demand substantial capital investment that may not align with short-term budget cycles, leaving gaps in immediate service resilience.
